newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman makes conciliatory speech to Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman makes conciliatory speech to Serbs.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman vowed on Monday to create conditions for all ethnic minorities to live in peace, in an unusually conciliatory speech to Serbs in their last remaining enclave of Croatia.

The address was his first response to demands by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright at the weekend that it was up to him to show "moral leadership" and create conditions for Serbs and Croats to live together in peace.
"We don't care for opening old wounds. We want to create conditions for the normal co-existence of all Croatian citizens," he told local Serb leaders in Eastern Slavonia.

"There will be...difficulties in making reconciliation work but I call upon all Croatian refugees and you, here, to find in yourselves political wisdom, so that we don't renew evil, so that we create better conditions for the lives of us and our children, so that such evil never happens again."

After his meeting Tudjman was jeered by a crowd of around 100 young men and prevented by security men from speaking to the public as he had planned. His comments were later broadcast on Croatian radio.

The visit followed municipal elections in April, in which local Serbs took part in a Croatian vote for the first time since 1991, when they went to war over Croatia's secession from federal Yugoslavia and seized around a third of the country.
They now control 11 of 28 municipalities in Eastern Slavonia.
Croatia recaptured all other Serb-held territory in a lightning offensive in 1995 and Eastern Slavonia is now home to thousands of Serbs who fled their advance.

The government plans to resettle tens of thousands of displaced people, but for Croats to return to Eastern Slavonia which they fled at the onset of war in 1991, the Serbs who live there must return to their own pre-war homes.

Recent attacks on Serbs who returned to their villages have provoked an angry response from the West and Albright told Tudjman it was morally unacceptable to have an ethnically pure state in modern-day Europe.

She said if he failed to act on U.S. demands, which include commitments made when he signed the 1995 Dayton peace accord that ended the war, the United States would consider blocking loans and Croatia's integration into Western institutions.
"Croatia will not travel the road to Europe unless all its peoples, Croats or Serbs, make the journey," she said.

Tudjman told Serb leaders on Monday Croatia would "make all possible efforts to heal the wounds of war. It won't be easy. The return of refugees demands patience, and it will evoke in some the remembrance of the evil they suffered."
He assured them the Croatian government supported the right of refugees to return home -- one of the cornerstones of the Dayton peace agreement.

Eastern Slavonia is administered by the United Nations, whose current mandate ends on July 15 when the area is due to come under Croatian government control. However the United States has hinted it might call for the current mandate covering 5,000 troops to be extended.

The U.N. Security Council will vote soon on whether the present mandate will be prolonged or reduced to a monitoring mission with fewer troops. Croatia has already agreed that some form of U.N. presence can remain until January next year.
Tudjman, who is expected to win a June 15 presidential election, met leaders of the Independent Serbian Democratic Party and the newly-elected Serb mayor of Beli Manastir.
